title: Road to Grandmaster
tagline: A Codeforces-only ladder that turns the Module 1 algorithm toolbox into rating — Newbie all the way to International Grandmaster. Every problem is real, curated by popularity, and grouped by the pattern it trains.

phases.title: Foundations
phases.summary: Get fast and accurate at the basics. The whole game here is reading carefully, coding cleanly, and not failing on edge cases. Aim to solve A/B of most Div.2 rounds on autopilot.

themes.title: Implementation & Simulation
themes.blurb: Most Div.2 A/B problems are just 'do exactly what the statement says, without bugs'. Speed and correctness here free up your clock for the harder problems later in the round.
signals: The statement describes a concrete process step by step.
Small constraints (n ≤ 2·10^5, often much smaller) and no obvious 'trick'.
You can already see the answer — the only risk is an off-by-one or an edge case.
themes.technique: Translate the statement into code literally, then hunt edge cases: empty input, n = 1, all-equal elements, max values (watch overflow → use 64-bit).
themes.trap: Rushing and missing a corner case. Re-read the constraints and the output format before submitting; a single wrong-answer on pretest 2 costs more time than a careful read.
themes.goal: Solve these in under 10 minutes each with zero penalty.

themes.title: Math & Parity Basics
themes.blurb: A huge fraction of easy problems collapse to one observation: parity, divisibility, a closed-form sum, or a gcd. Train yourself to look for the formula first.
signals: Answer asked for huge n — you can't simulate, you must find a formula.
Words like 'even/odd', 'divisible', 'multiple of', 'sum of first k'.
Tiny output (a single number) from large input.
themes.technique: Compute small cases by hand, spot the pattern, prove it with parity/divisibility/arithmetic-series reasoning. Keep gcd, lcm and n(n+1)/2 in muscle memory.
themes.trap: Integer overflow on the closed form — sums of n up to 1e9 overflow 32-bit. Use 64-bit everywhere.
themes.goal: See the formula within 2–3 small examples instead of coding a loop.

problems.name: Arpa’s hard exam and Mehrdad’s naive cheat

themes.title: First Greedy Moves
themes.blurb: Sort, then take the best available choice. Easy greedies are about *ordering* the input the right way and proving the obvious move is safe.
signals: 'Maximize / minimize' with no dependency between choices.
Sorting the input makes the decision obvious.
Each step has a clearly 'best' local option.
themes.technique: Sort by the right key, then sweep. Ask 'why is taking the best item now never wrong?' — that's your exchange argument.
themes.trap: Greedy that *feels* right but isn't. If you can't argue why a local choice is globally safe, suspect DP.
themes.goal: Recognise the sort key instantly.

themes.title: Brute Force & Search Spaces
themes.blurb: When n is tiny, just try everything. The skill is recognising that the search space is small enough (2^n, n!, or n^2/n^3) to enumerate.
signals: n ≤ 20 → subsets (2^n).  n ≤ 10 → permutations (n!).
Constraints far smaller than usual — the setter is inviting brute force.
'Choose some subset / arrangement that...'
themes.technique: Estimate the work: 2^n, n!, or nested loops. If it fits ~10^8, enumerate and check each candidate.
themes.trap: Misjudging the size — 2^25 is 3·10^7 (fine), 2^40 is not. Always do the back-of-envelope count first.
themes.goal: Map constraints → enumeration size in seconds.

themes.title: Two Pointers & Sorting Tricks
themes.blurb: After sorting, a pair of indices sweeping the array answers a surprising number of 'find a pair / a window' questions in linear time.
signals: 'Find two elements with sum / difference X' on a sortable array.
'Longest / shortest contiguous segment such that ...'.
Monotonic relationship: moving one pointer only ever moves the other one way.
themes.technique: Sort if order doesn't matter, then advance L/R based on whether the current window is too big or too small.
themes.trap: Using two pointers when the window condition isn't monotonic — then you need a different tool.
themes.goal: Reach for sort + two pointers reflexively on pair/window prompts.

phases.title: Climbing to Specialist
phases.summary: Now C-level problems need a real idea. This phase is where binary search, prefix sums, constructive thinking and basic graph/DP first appear. Pattern recognition starts paying off hard here.

themes.title: Binary Search
themes.blurb: Binary search on a sorted array — and, more powerfully, on the *answer*. If a boolean check is monotonic, you can binary search the smallest/largest value that passes.
signals: 'Minimum / maximum value such that some condition holds.'
A check(x) that is monotonic: false…false,true…true.
Sorted data + 'how many ≤ x' style queries.
themes.technique: Define check(x) carefully, prove monotonicity, then standard lo/hi loop. Decide [lo,hi) vs [lo,hi] and stick to it.
themes.trap: Off-by-one in the boundary and an infinite loop when lo/hi don't converge. Write the invariant down.
themes.goal: Spot 'binary search the answer' from the phrase 'minimum maximum'.

themes.title: Constructive Algorithms
themes.blurb: Codeforces' signature genre: 'construct ANY valid object'. There's no search — you invent a pattern that always works and prove it does.
signals: 'Construct any array/permutation/grid such that ...'.
Often 'print -1 if impossible' — first nail the impossibility condition.
Small examples in the statement that hint at a repeating structure.
themes.technique: Play with n=1,2,3 by hand, find a repeatable pattern (alternate, pair up, snake, halve), then argue it always satisfies the constraints.
themes.trap: Forgetting the -1 case, or a construction that breaks on the smallest n. Always test n=1 and n=2.
themes.goal: Build intuition for 'invent a pattern' problems — these are free rating once it clicks.

themes.title: Number Theory Basics
themes.blurb: Primes, divisors, gcd and modular arithmetic. The sieve and divisor enumeration in √n unlock most early number-theory problems.
signals: 'Count divisors / primes', 'is it prime', 'gcd of subarray'.
Numbers up to 10^6 → precompute a sieve / smallest prime factor.
Anything 'modulo 10^9+7'.
themes.technique: Sieve for primality/factorisation up to 1e6; trial-divide to √n for a single number; use gcd identities for subarray-gcd tricks.
themes.trap: O(n) divisor loops when √n suffices; forgetting that gcd of a range only ever decreases.
themes.goal: Know instantly whether to sieve or trial-divide.

problems.name: Omkar and Last Class of Math

themes.title: Greedy + Sorting
themes.blurb: The workhorse combo: sort by a clever key, then make the locally optimal choice. The hard part is choosing the key and proving the exchange argument.
signals: Pairing / scheduling / assigning to minimise or maximise a total.
Two arrays you can reorder independently.
'If I swap two adjacent choices, the answer doesn't improve.'
themes.technique: Guess a sort key, then prove with an exchange argument: any optimal solution can be reordered to match the greedy without getting worse.
themes.trap: Sorting by the wrong attribute (e.g. by deadline vs by length). Test the greedy against brute force on tiny inputs.
themes.goal: Derive and trust the exchange argument under contest pressure.

problems.name: Anna and the Valentine's Day Gift

themes.title: Graph Traversal (BFS / DFS)
themes.blurb: Connected components, flood fill, shortest path in an unweighted graph, cycle detection. BFS/DFS is the backbone of half of CP.
signals: Grid or explicit graph; 'connected regions', 'reachable', 'components'.
Unweighted shortest path → plain BFS.
'Is there a cycle', 'is it bipartite', 'color the graph'.
themes.technique: Model the state as nodes/edges, pick BFS (layers / shortest steps) or DFS (connectivity / recursion), and track a visited set.
themes.trap: Recursion-depth stack overflow on big graphs (use an explicit stack / iterative DFS); revisiting nodes without a visited check.
themes.goal: Translate a word problem into a graph automatically.

problems.name: Mahmoud and Ehab and the bipartiteness

themes.title: Intro Dynamic Programming
themes.blurb: 1-D DP: count ways, min cost, can-you-reach. The leap is seeing the problem as a sequence of decisions with overlapping subproblems.
signals: 'Number of ways', 'minimum cost', 'can you reach' with sequential choices.
Exponential brute force that obviously repeats subproblems.
Choice at step i depends only on a few earlier states.
themes.technique: Define dp[i] in words first ('best answer using first i'), write the transition, set the base case, decide iteration order.
themes.trap: Wrong base case / iteration order, or a state that doesn't capture enough information. State design is 80% of DP.
themes.goal: Phrase a clean dp[i] definition before touching code.

problems.name: Given Length and Sum of Digits...

phases.title: Becoming Expert
phases.summary: The Expert wall. Problems now combine two ideas: binary-search-on-answer with a greedy check, DP with bitmasks, graphs with DSU. This is where deliberate pattern practice separates Experts from stuck Specialists.

themes.title: Binary Search on the Answer
themes.blurb: The classic Expert combo: binary search the answer, and the feasibility check is itself a greedy or simulation. Recognising the monotonic check is the whole skill.
signals: 'Maximise the minimum' or 'minimise the maximum'.
Splitting / allocating with a threshold that gets easier as the threshold relaxes.
A check(x) you can verify greedily in O(n).
themes.technique: Binary search x; write a greedy check(x). Prove that if x works, so does every easier x (monotonicity).
themes.trap: A check that isn't actually monotonic, or an O(n log n) check that makes the whole thing too slow.
themes.goal: Decompose into 'search the value' + 'greedy verify'.

themes.title: Classic DP Patterns
themes.blurb: Knapsack, LIS, LCS, partition, grid DP — the named patterns. Most mid-level DP is one of these wearing a costume.
signals: Subset-sum / 'pick items under a budget' → knapsack.
'Longest increasing / common subsequence' → LIS / LCS.
2-D grid with moves → grid DP.
themes.technique: Match to the closest named pattern, then adapt the state. Remember LIS in O(n log n) via patience sorting / lower_bound.
themes.trap: Memory blowup on 2-D DP — roll the array to one row when only the previous row is needed.
themes.goal: Instantly classify which classic pattern fits.

themes.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
themes.blurb: Union-Find answers 'are these connected?' under merges, near-instantly. It also powers Kruskal's MST and offline connectivity tricks.
signals: Edges added over time; 'are u and v connected now?'.
Counting / sizing connected components after unions.
Kruskal MST, or grouping elements by an equivalence relation.
themes.technique: Path compression + union by size/rank → near-O(1). For 'connectivity over deletions', process queries offline in reverse.
themes.trap: Forgetting to union by size/rank (degrades to O(n)); using find without path compression.
themes.goal: See merges-over-time → DSU automatically.

themes.title: Weighted Shortest Paths
themes.blurb: Dijkstra (non-negative), Bellman-Ford (negative edges / k steps), Floyd-Warshall (all pairs, small n). Pick by the edge weights and graph size.
signals: Weighted edges + 'shortest / cheapest path'.
Non-negative weights → Dijkstra; negative or 'at most k edges' → Bellman-Ford.
n ≤ 500 and all-pairs distances → Floyd-Warshall.
themes.technique: Dijkstra with a heap and stale-entry skipping; sometimes the state is (node, extra) — a layered graph. Floyd-Warshall for transitive-closure style problems.
themes.trap: Running Dijkstra with negative edges; 32-bit overflow on summed weights.
themes.goal: Choose the right shortest-path algorithm from weights + n.

problems.name: Lunar New Year and a Wander

themes.title: Modular Arithmetic & Number Theory
themes.blurb: Fast exponentiation, modular inverses, factorisation by smallest-prime, and counting with divisors. The mod 10^9+7 toolkit.
signals: 'Compute X mod p' for huge X, or a^b mod p.
Division under a modulus → modular inverse (Fermat).
Counting multiples / coprimes / divisor sums.
themes.technique: Binary exponentiation for powers and inverses; precompute smallest-prime-factor for fast factorisation; inclusion–exclusion over prime factors.
themes.trap: Negative values mod p (normalise with ((x%p)+p)%p); inverse of a non-coprime number.
themes.goal: Fluent modular algebra under contest time.

themes.title: String Matching & Hashing
themes.blurb: Prefix-functions (KMP), Z-array, and polynomial hashing turn substring questions into O(n). Hashing is the universal 'are these equal?' hammer.
signals: 'Does pattern occur', 'count occurrences', 'longest border/period'.
Compare many substrings for equality → polynomial hashing.
Prefix = suffix structure → KMP failure function / Z.
themes.technique: KMP/Z for occurrences and periods; double hashing (two mods) to kill collisions; precompute prefix hashes for O(1) substring compares.
themes.trap: Single-mod hash collisions on adversarial tests; mismatched base/mod between strings.
themes.goal: Reduce substring questions to hashing or a prefix function.

themes.title: Bit Tricks & Bitmask Enumeration
themes.blurb: Treat a set / small array as the bits of an integer. XOR/AND/OR identities and subset enumeration solve a whole class of 'choose a subset' problems.
signals: n ≤ 20–22 and 'choose a subset / partition'.
XOR-based conditions, 'pair up so that ...'.
Bitwise AND/OR/XOR of a range or subset.
themes.technique: Iterate masks 0..2^n-1; enumerate submasks with the (m-1)&mask trick; reason bit-by-bit for AND/OR/XOR constraints (each bit independent).
themes.trap: Confusing submask vs supermask iteration; forgetting bit independence simplifies the problem.
themes.goal: Map 'small set' problems to integer bitmasks.

themes.title: Sliding Window & Prefix Sums
themes.blurb: A window that grows/shrinks to maintain an invariant, backed by prefix sums for O(1) range queries. The linear-time answer to many 'segment' problems.
signals: 'Longest / number of subarrays with property P' where P is monotonic in length.
Range-sum queries → prefix sums (or prefix XOR / counts).
Count pairs (i,j) with a sum/condition via a running map.
themes.technique: Expand right, shrink left while the window violates P; precompute prefix arrays so any range is O(1).
themes.trap: Non-monotonic conditions break the window; prefix-sum overflow.
themes.goal: Default to window + prefix sums on subarray prompts.

themes.title: Counting & Combinatorics
themes.blurb: Count arrangements with nCr, the stars-and-bars trick, and inclusion–exclusion — all under a modulus with precomputed factorials.
signals: 'How many ways / arrangements / sequences', answer mod p.
Distribute identical items → stars and bars.
'At least one' / 'none of' constraints → inclusion–exclusion.
themes.technique: Precompute factorials + inverse factorials for O(1) nCr mod p; decompose the count into independent choices; subtract bad cases with inclusion–exclusion.
themes.trap: Forgetting modular inverse for division; double counting symmetric arrangements.
themes.goal: Break a count into independent multiplicative choices.

phases.title: The Candidate Master Push
phases.summary: The target tier. Data structures (segment trees / Fenwick), tree DP, advanced DP states, and SCC-level graph theory. Problems reward a deep toolbox plus the judgement to combine tools. This is the heart of the roadmap.

themes.title: Segment Trees & Fenwick
themes.blurb: Point-update / range-query in O(log n). Fenwick for sums and inversion counting; segment trees for min/max/gcd and more. The CM-level data-structure backbone.
signals: Many range queries + point updates interleaved.
Count inversions / 'elements smaller to the right' → Fenwick.
Range min/max/sum/gcd with updates → segment tree.
themes.technique: Fenwick for prefix-aggregate + point update; segment tree for any associative range op; coordinate-compress when values are large.
themes.trap: Off-by-one in 1-indexed Fenwick; forgetting to compress coordinates.
themes.goal: Reach for a BIT/segtree the moment you see range query + update.

themes.title: Tree Algorithms & LCA
themes.blurb: Rooting, subtree sizes, diameter, LCA, and distance queries. The standard tree toolkit that shows up in nearly every CM round.
signals: Input is a tree (n nodes, n-1 edges).
'Distance between u and v', 'kth ancestor' → LCA (binary lifting).
'Longest path' → diameter via two BFS / DFS.
themes.technique: Root the tree, compute subtree sizes / depths with one DFS; binary-lifting LCA for distance and ancestor queries.
themes.trap: Recursion depth on a path-shaped tree (10^5 deep) → iterative DFS or raise the limit.
themes.goal: Apply the rooted-tree toolkit on sight.

themes.title: DP on Trees
themes.blurb: Combine children's answers into the parent's. Add rerooting to get the answer for every node in O(n). A signature CM skill.
signals: Tree + 'best/count over subtrees' or 'for every root'.
Answer at a node depends on its children's answers.
'Maximum independent set / matching / path' on a tree.
themes.technique: Post-order DFS to fold children up; for 'answer for all roots', do a second DFS passing the parent's contribution down (rerooting).
themes.trap: Mixing up which child contributions to exclude during rerooting; deep recursion.
themes.goal: Design subtree states and reroot confidently.

problems.name: A and B and Lecture Rooms

themes.title: Advanced DP States
themes.blurb: Bitmask DP over subsets, interval DP, and digit DP. The state stops being a single index and becomes a richer object — the key creative leap to CM.
signals: n ≤ 20 with 'visit all / assign all' → bitmask DP (TSP-like).
'Combine adjacent segments optimally' → interval DP.
'Count numbers ≤ N with a digit property' → digit DP.
themes.technique: Bitmask DP: dp[mask] over visited sets. Interval DP: dp[l][r] over a split point. Digit DP: dp[pos][tight][state] over the decimal expansion.
themes.trap: 2^n · n blowing the time budget; forgetting the 'tight' flag in digit DP.
themes.goal: Recognise which non-trivial DP state the problem needs.

themes.title: SCC, Topo & Graph Structure
themes.blurb: Condense a directed graph into its strongly-connected components, then work on the resulting DAG. Topological order powers DAG DP and dependency problems.
signals: Directed graph with cycles you want to collapse.
'Group mutually reachable nodes', 'minimum to make strongly connected'.
DAG + longest/critical path → topo-order DP.
themes.technique: Tarjan / Kosaraju for SCC → condensation DAG; topological sort then DP along the order. Implication graphs (2-SAT flavour) reduce to SCC.
themes.trap: Treating the original graph as a DAG before condensing; cycle handling in topo sort.
themes.goal: Condense to a DAG, then solve on the DAG.

themes.title: Hard Constructive & Greedy
themes.blurb: CM-level constructive: the pattern is subtle and the proof matters. These build the 'invent + justify' muscle that defines a strong Expert/CM.
signals: 'Construct such that ...' with a non-obvious global constraint.
Interactive or adaptive flavour, or a tight bound on operations.
A clean answer once you spot the right invariant.
themes.technique: Find an invariant the construction must preserve; build greedily while maintaining it; prove optimality / validity by that invariant.
themes.trap: A construction that passes small cases but violates the bound at scale. Stress-test against brute force.
themes.goal: Invent and *prove* constructions under pressure.

themes.title: Harder Math & Probability
themes.blurb: Expected value, probability, and combinatorial identities — usually mod p. Linearity of expectation turns scary problems into a sum of easy ones.
signals: 'Expected value of ...', 'probability that ...'.
A sum over all pairs / subsets that you can swap order on.
Counting with symmetry → Burnside-lite reasoning.
themes.technique: Linearity of expectation: sum each element's contribution independently; swap summation order; combinatorial identities to collapse sums.
themes.trap: Treating dependent events as independent; modular inverse of probabilities.
themes.goal: Reach for linearity of expectation reflexively.

phases.title: Candidate Master
phases.summary: The CM threshold. The tools don't change — the combinations and the proofs get sharper. This tier is intentionally wide: drill every Module-1 family at 1900–2100 until the patterns fire automatically and your implementation is clean under pressure.

themes.title: Dynamic Programming
themes.blurb: DP at the CM line: the state design is the puzzle. Most of these hide a knapsack, an LIS, an interval split, or a clever index behind a new costume.
signals: A brute force that obviously repeats overlapping subproblems.
Sequential choices where the future depends on a small summary of the past.
'Count / minimise / maximise over arrangements' with n large enough to rule out brute force.
themes.technique: Write dp[state] in words before code; minimise the state to exactly what the transition needs; pick the iteration order so dependencies are ready.
themes.trap: An under-specified state that loses information, or an order that reads dp cells before they're computed.
themes.goal: Design a correct, minimal DP state in one pass.

themes.title: Segment Trees & Fenwick
themes.blurb: Range query + update under O(log n). At this level the data structure is often the easy part — spotting that the problem reduces to range ops is the skill.
signals: Interleaved range queries and updates over an array.
Counting 'how many earlier elements satisfy …' → BIT over compressed values.
A DP transition that is really a range max/sum lookup.
themes.technique: Fenwick for prefix aggregates; segment tree for any associative op; coordinate-compress big values; sweep events left-to-right.
themes.trap: Forgetting coordinate compression; 1-indexed BIT off-by-ones; non-associative ops on a segment tree.
themes.goal: Reduce the problem to range query + update on sight.

themes.title: Trees & Tree DP
themes.blurb: Subtree DP, rerooting, LCA and distance arguments. Tree problems reward a fixed mental checklist: root it, get sizes/depths, fold children up.
signals: Input is a tree; the answer combines children into the parent.
'For every node' answers → rerooting in O(n).
Distance / ancestor queries → binary-lifting LCA.
themes.technique: Post-order DFS to fold subtree answers; a second top-down pass to reroot; binary lifting for LCA and kth-ancestor.
themes.trap: Recursion depth on a path-shaped tree; mishandling which child to exclude when rerooting.
themes.goal: Apply the rooted-tree checklist reflexively.

themes.title: Graphs & Shortest Paths
themes.blurb: Modelling is the battle: turn the prose into nodes and edges, then it's Dijkstra, DSU, topo-order, or an SCC condensation you already know.
signals: States with transitions → a (possibly layered) graph.
Merges over time / connectivity → DSU; directed cycles to collapse → SCC.
Weighted shortest path → Dijkstra; dependencies → topological order.
themes.technique: Define the state graph explicitly; pick BFS/Dijkstra/DSU/SCC by the structure; build the condensation DAG when cycles get in the way.
themes.trap: Hidden state in the node (e.g. parity) you forgot to encode; 0/1-BFS vs Dijkstra confusion.
themes.goal: Translate any process into the right graph instantly.

themes.title: Strings & Hashing
themes.blurb: Prefix functions, Z, and polynomial hashing reduce substring questions to O(n). Hashing is the universal equality hammer once collisions are controlled.
signals: Occurrences, borders, periods → KMP / Z.
Many substring equality checks → prefix hashes (double-mod).
Lexicographic / distinct-substring questions → suffix array + LCP.
themes.technique: Precompute prefix hashes for O(1) compares; KMP/Z for periodicity; suffix array + LCP for ordering and counting.
themes.trap: Single-mod hash collisions on adversarial tests; mismatched base/mod across strings.
themes.goal: Map substring questions to a prefix function or hash.

themes.title: Counting & Combinatorics
themes.blurb: Decompose a count into independent multiplicative choices, with nCr, stars and bars, and inclusion–exclusion — all mod p with precomputed factorials.
signals: 'How many ways / sequences / arrangements', answer mod p.
Distribute identical items → stars and bars.
'At least one' / 'none of' → inclusion–exclusion.
themes.technique: Precompute factorials + inverse factorials for O(1) nCr; split into independent choices; subtract bad cases with inclusion–exclusion.
themes.trap: Division without modular inverse; double counting symmetric configurations.
themes.goal: Factor a count into independent choices fast.

problems.name: Sasha and a Walk in the City

themes.title: Number Theory
themes.blurb: Sieve / smallest-prime factorisation, modular inverses, divisor sums and gcd structure. The mod-p toolkit applied to harder counting and divisibility.
signals: Factorise many numbers ≤ 1e6 → precompute smallest prime factor.
Counting coprimes / multiples → inclusion–exclusion over prime factors.
Division under a modulus → Fermat inverse.
themes.technique: Linear sieve for SPF; binary exponentiation for powers/inverses; inclusion–exclusion over the prime factorisation.
themes.trap: Negative residues mod p; inverse of a non-coprime value; overflow before the mod.
themes.goal: Fluent factorisation + modular algebra.

problems.name: Bash and a Tough Math Puzzle

themes.title: Bitmask & Meet-in-the-Middle
themes.blurb: Small sets become integers. Bitmask DP over subsets, submask enumeration, and splitting n in half (meet-in-the-middle) to beat 2^n.
signals: n ≤ 20–22 with 'assign / visit all' → bitmask DP.
n ≤ 40 'choose a subset with target sum' → meet in the middle.
Per-bit independent AND/OR/XOR constraints.
themes.technique: dp[mask] over visited sets; submask loop with (m-1)&mask; split into two halves and merge sorted partial sums.
themes.trap: 2^n·n exceeding the budget; submask vs supermask iteration mix-ups.
themes.goal: See 'small set' / 'n≈40' → bitmask or MITM.

themes.title: Constructive & Greedy
themes.blurb: Invent a pattern that always works and prove it. CM-level constructive needs an invariant and a clean greedy that maintains it.
signals: 'Construct any … such that', often with a -1 impossibility case.
A tight bound on the number of operations.
Small examples hinting at a repeating structure.
themes.technique: Find the invariant the answer must preserve; build greedily maintaining it; pin the impossibility condition first.
themes.trap: A construction that breaks at the smallest n or violates the op bound at scale — stress-test it.
themes.goal: Invent and justify constructions under time pressure.

themes.title: Binary Search & Two Pointers
themes.blurb: Binary search the answer with a greedy/sim check, or sweep two pointers over a monotone window. The decomposition into 'search value + verify' is the move.
signals: 'Maximise the minimum' / 'minimise the maximum'.
A monotone check(x) verifiable in O(n).
Longest/shortest window with a monotone property.
themes.technique: Binary search x with a greedy check; prove monotonicity; or expand/shrink a two-pointer window maintaining the invariant.
themes.trap: A check that isn't truly monotonic; an O(n log n) check making the whole thing too slow.
themes.goal: Split into 'search the value' + 'verify greedily'.

phases.title: Master
phases.summary: Master tier (orange). Problems now layer techniques: a data structure inside a DP, a greedy inside a binary search, a counting argument with a structural twist. Solving these consistently is a 2100+ rating.

themes.title: Hard Dynamic Programming
themes.blurb: Multi-dimensional states, DP over structure, and transitions that need a second idea to compute efficiently. State design plus a transition trick.
signals: The obvious DP is correct but a dimension or transition is too slow.
State = (position, some compressed summary, tight/parity flag).
Counting DP whose transition is itself an aggregate.
themes.technique: Nail the minimal state, then attack the transition: prefix sums, monotonic structure, or a small data structure to speed it.
themes.trap: A state that's one dimension too big; recomputing transitions that could be accumulated.
themes.goal: Find the extra idea that makes a correct DP fast.

themes.title: Advanced Data Structures
themes.blurb: Lazy propagation, segment-tree-on-DP, BIT-of-BIT, and offline sweeps. The structure encodes the whole problem; correctness lives in the tag algebra.
signals: Range assign/add + range aggregate, repeated.
Offline queries you can sort by one coordinate and sweep.
A DP recurrence equal to a range operation over an index.
themes.technique: Compose lazy tags carefully and push down before recursing; sort queries offline; encode the DP transition as a segment-tree op.
themes.trap: Tag composition order; forgetting push-down on queries; merge step that isn't associative.
themes.goal: Express the problem as clean range operations.

themes.title: Hard Tree Problems
themes.blurb: Rerooting with non-trivial merges, small-to-large, Euler-tour + BIT, and auxiliary/virtual-tree ideas. Tree structure exploited to the hilt.
signals: Aggregate over all paths / all subtrees with a heavy merge.
Subtree queries → Euler tour flattening + a BIT/segment tree.
Per-node answers needing both downward and upward information.
themes.technique: Euler-tour to turn subtrees into ranges; small-to-large for set merges; reroot with an invertible combine.
themes.trap: Small-to-large without the size check (loses the log); Euler-tour index bugs.
themes.goal: Reach for Euler-tour / small-to-large when subtree-DP stalls.

problems.name: Minimum spanning tree for each edge

themes.title: Graph Theory
themes.blurb: SCC condensation, DSU on the MST / Kruskal reconstruction, layered shortest paths, and implication graphs. The structural graph toolbox at Master level.
signals: Directed cycles to collapse → SCC + DAG DP.
Bottleneck / 'minimise the max edge on a path' → MST / Kruskal reconstruction.
Constraints of the form 'a OR b' → 2-SAT-style implication graph (reduces to SCC).
themes.technique: Condense to a DAG and DP on it; build the reconstruction tree from Kruskal; model implications as a graph and run SCC.
themes.trap: Treating a cyclic graph as a DAG; missing that bottleneck paths live on the MST.
themes.goal: Pick the structural reduction the graph is hinting at.

problems.name: Turtle and a MEX Problem (Hard Version)
To Go Or Not To Go?

themes.title: Heavy Strings
themes.blurb: Suffix arrays/automata and hashing fused with data structures. Distinct substrings, longest common/repeated, and query-heavy substring problems.
signals: 'Number of distinct substrings', 'longest repeated/common substring'.
Substring queries answered offline across many positions.
Periodicity + ranges combined.
themes.technique: Suffix array + LCP (or suffix automaton) for counting/ordering; combine hashing with a BIT/segment tree for queries.
themes.trap: Suffix-structure constant factor timing out; hash collisions at scale.
themes.goal: Choose the suffix structure that matches the query type.

problems.name: Kirk and a Binary String (hard version)

themes.title: Advanced Counting
themes.blurb: Counting fused with DP and inclusion–exclusion: count configurations, count with forbidden patterns, count over structures — proofs you must trust.
signals: 'Count valid X' where X has rich internal structure.
DP whose value is a count, combined with binomials.
Inclusion–exclusion layered over a DP or over constraints.
themes.technique: Set up a counting DP, fold in nCr factors, subtract invalid configurations by inclusion–exclusion; exploit symmetry.
themes.trap: Inclusion–exclusion sign/term errors; overcounting symmetric objects.
themes.goal: Fuse combinatorial identities with a DP cleanly.

themes.title: Deep Number Theory
themes.blurb: Multiplicative functions, Möbius/CRT-flavoured counting, and divisor-sum manipulation. Number theory where the identity is the whole solution.
signals: Sums over gcd / divisors that beg for Möbius or divisor sieving.
Independent constraints modulo coprime numbers → CRT.
Counting via multiplicative structure.
themes.technique: Divisor sieve to aggregate over multiples; Möbius inversion for coprime counting; CRT to merge modular constraints.
themes.trap: Forgetting multiplicativity preconditions; overflow in divisor sums.
themes.goal: Recognise gcd/divisor sums → Möbius / divisor sieve.

themes.title: DP Optimisation & Divide-and-Conquer
themes.blurb: Drop an O(n^2) DP to O(n log n): divide-and-conquer optimisation, convex-hull trick, Knuth — and D&C as a technique (inversions, CDQ).
signals: dp[i] = min(dp[j] + cost(j,i)) with a monotone optimal j.
Cost obeys the quadrangle inequality → Knuth / D&C opt.
Count cross-pairs over a split → divide and conquer.
themes.technique: Prove monotonicity of the optimal split and recurse over it; maintain lines for CHT; merge-count cross-pairs in O(n).
themes.trap: Applying an optimisation without checking its monotonicity/convexity precondition.
themes.goal: Spot the structure that unlocks a faster DP.

themes.title: Probability & Expectation
themes.blurb: Expected value and probability, usually mod p. Linearity of expectation turns a frightening global quantity into a sum of tiny independent contributions.
signals: 'Expected value / probability that …'.
A global random quantity that decomposes per element / per pair.
Markov-chain-like transitions on a small state space.
themes.technique: Linearity of expectation: sum each contribution independently; set up and solve the linear system / DP over states; keep probabilities as modular fractions.
themes.trap: Assuming independence that isn't there; modular inverse of probabilities.
themes.goal: Decompose expectations by linearity automatically.

problems.name: LuoTianyi and the Floating Islands (Hard Version)

themes.title: Matrix Exponentiation
themes.blurb: Evaluate a linear recurrence at enormous n by raising its transition matrix to the n-th power in O(k^3 log n) — also counts fixed-length walks in a small graph.
signals: Linear recurrence wanted at n up to 1e18.
'Number of walks of length n' in a small graph.
A state vector advanced by the same linear map each step.
themes.technique: Encode the transition as a matrix and binary-exponentiate it under the modulus; adjacency-matrix powers count walks.
themes.trap: Cubic multiply too slow when k is large; modular overflow in the product.
themes.goal: See 'linear recurrence at huge n' → matrix power.

problems.name: Mahmoud and Ehab and yet another xor task

phases.title: Grandmaster
phases.summary: Grandmaster territory (red). Each problem needs a genuine insight plus flawless implementation of a heavy technique. Fewer per theme — every one is a serious sitting. Still built entirely from the Module-1 toolbox, taken much deeper.

themes.title: Grandmaster DP
themes.blurb: DP where even seeing the state is hard: profile/broken-profile DP, DP on subsets with extra structure, and transitions that need their own algorithm.
signals: The state is an object (a profile, a partition, a set with metadata).
A correct DP whose transition is itself a non-trivial computation.
Optimisation only possible after reformulating the recurrence.
themes.technique: Reformulate until the state is minimal and the transition is a known fast operation; layer prefix sums / data structures inside the transition.
themes.trap: Locking onto the first state you think of; missing a reformulation that halves a dimension.
themes.goal: Reformulate DPs until they become tractable.

problems.name: Sonya and Problem Wihtout a Legend

themes.title: Heavy Data Structures
themes.blurb: Segment tree beats, persistent structures, merge-sort tree, and DSU-on-tree. The structure is intricate and the proof of its complexity matters.
signals: Range operations with a non-obvious potential/amortised bound.
Historic / versioned queries → persistence.
Offline tree queries → DSU on tree (small-to-large on counts).
themes.technique: Reach for beats / persistence / merge-sort tree by the query type; argue the amortised or O(n log^2) bound explicitly.
themes.trap: Hand-waving the complexity of a beats/amortised structure; memory blowup in persistence.
themes.goal: Match an exotic structure to the query and prove its bound.

themes.title: Advanced Trees
themes.blurb: Centroid decomposition, heavy-light, auxiliary/virtual trees, and DSU-on-tree. Path and subtree problems that need a genuine tree-decomposition.
signals: Count/aggregate over all paths → centroid decomposition.
Path queries with updates → heavy-light + segment tree.
Queries on a small set of important nodes → virtual tree.
themes.technique: Centroid decomposition for path counting; HLD to map paths to ranges; build the virtual tree on the relevant nodes.
themes.trap: Centroid recursion bugs / double counting through the centroid; HLD index errors.
themes.goal: Select the right tree decomposition for the query.

themes.title: Hard Graph Theory
themes.blurb: SCC/2-SAT reductions, MST reconstruction trees, small-to-large on components, and shortest paths with exotic state. Deep structural graph reasoning.
signals: Boolean constraints 'a OR b' → 2-SAT via SCC.
Queries about the min/max edge on paths → Kruskal reconstruction tree.
Offline connectivity over edge insertions/deletions → DSU tricks.
themes.technique: Reduce to SCC where possible; build the reconstruction tree; process connectivity offline; layer state into the graph nodes.
themes.trap: Incorrect 2-SAT implication edges; assuming online when an offline DSU is intended.
themes.goal: Find the reduction that turns the graph tractable.

themes.title: Suffix Structures
themes.blurb: Suffix automaton/array, Aho-Corasick-style multi-pattern reasoning, and hashing fused with heavy data structures. The top end of string algorithmics.
signals: Counting distinct substrings / occurrences across many patterns.
Substring statistics over the suffix-automaton DAG.
Lexicographic structure exploited with a data structure.
themes.technique: Suffix automaton for substring counting; suffix array + LCP for ordering; combine with segment trees / BIT for query aggregation.
themes.trap: Suffix-automaton transition/clone bugs; constant factor timing out.
themes.goal: Wield suffix structures as a routine tool.

themes.title: Counting Masterclass
themes.blurb: Generating-function thinking, layered inclusion–exclusion, and counting over complex structures. Where the right algebraic manipulation is the whole problem.
signals: A count that resists direct DP but telescopes algebraically.
Inclusion–exclusion nested several levels deep.
Symmetry you can quotient out (Burnside-style).
themes.technique: Model with generating functions / convolutions; apply layered inclusion–exclusion; collapse sums with combinatorial identities.
themes.trap: Sign/term bookkeeping in deep inclusion–exclusion; missing a symmetry.
themes.goal: Reach for the algebraic reformulation of a count.

themes.title: Number Theory Masterclass
themes.blurb: Möbius inversion, multiplicative-function sieves, primitive roots and discrete logs. Number theory where a deep identity collapses the whole computation.
signals: Sums over gcd/divisors at scale → Möbius / Dirichlet.
Order / primitive-root structure modulo p.
Counting with multiplicative functions.
themes.technique: Möbius inversion and divisor sieves to aggregate; precompute multiplicative functions; use orders / discrete log where the group structure helps.
themes.trap: Multiplicativity assumed where it fails; precision/overflow in large sieved sums.
themes.goal: Collapse number-theoretic sums with the right identity.

themes.title: Divide & Conquer / DP-Opt
themes.blurb: CDQ divide-and-conquer over time, divide-and-conquer DP optimisation, and parallel binary search. Offline machinery that turns hard queries linear-ish.
signals: Offline queries + updates orderable by time → CDQ.
Answer-monotone queries solvable together → parallel binary search.
dp split point monotone in the outer index → D&C opt.
themes.technique: CDQ: recurse on time, apply left updates to right queries; parallel binary search across all queries at once; D&C over the monotone optimal split.
themes.trap: Mixing update/query order across the CDQ split; non-monotone assumptions.
themes.goal: Recognise when offline D&C machinery applies.

problems.name: Max to the Right of Min

themes.title: Grandmaster Constructive
themes.blurb: Constructions with deep invariants and tight proofs, often interactive or adaptive. The 'invent + prove' muscle at its strongest.
signals: 'Construct …' with a subtle global constraint and an operation budget.
Interactive/adaptive judging.
A clean answer once the right invariant is found.
themes.technique: Hunt the invariant; build incrementally maintaining it; prove validity and the bound; stress-test against brute force.
themes.trap: A construction that passes small cases but breaks the bound at scale.
themes.goal: Invent and rigorously justify hard constructions.

phases.title: International Grandmaster
phases.summary: The summit. 2600+ problems are among the hardest Codeforces has produced — yet they are still assembled from the Module-1 toolbox pushed to its absolute limit. Treat each as a mini research problem: expect to spend hours, and to learn something every time.

themes.title: Frontier DP
themes.blurb: DP at the edge of the field: deep reformulations, connection-profile DP, and recurrences that only become tractable after a hard structural observation.
signals: A count/optimum with no obvious state until you reframe the object.
Transitions hiding another full algorithm.
Optimisation possible only after an algebraic or structural rewrite.
themes.technique: Reframe relentlessly; compress the state; embed convolutions / data structures / matrix powers inside the transition.
themes.trap: Committing to a state before exploring reformulations; under-estimating the transition cost.
themes.goal: Turn an intractable-looking count into a clean recurrence.

themes.title: Extreme Data Structures
themes.blurb: Persistent + amortised hybrids, segment tree beats with subtle potentials, and offline machinery with delicate complexity proofs.
signals: Range ops whose efficiency rests on a non-obvious potential function.
Versioned + range + order-statistic queries combined.
Complexity only justified by amortised analysis.
themes.technique: Combine persistence, beats, and offline sweeps; prove the amortised / O(n log^2) bound carefully; compress aggressively.
themes.trap: Unproven complexity; memory limits on persistence; tag-algebra subtleties.
themes.goal: Engineer and justify a bespoke heavy structure.

problems.name: Arpa’s letter-marked tree and Mehrdad’s Dokhtar-kosh paths

themes.title: Frontier Graph Theory
themes.blurb: Deep structural graph problems: layered SCC reductions, reconstruction-tree queries, and shortest paths over richly augmented state spaces.
signals: A reduction to SCC / DSU that itself takes work to see.
Path-extremal queries over an MST reconstruction tree.
State graphs with many augmenting dimensions.
themes.technique: Find the reduction, then apply the known machinery flawlessly; augment node state minimally; exploit the reconstruction tree.
themes.trap: Wrong reduction; exploding the augmented state space.
themes.goal: See the hidden reduction in a hard graph problem.

problems.name: Arpa’s overnight party and Mehrdad’s silent entering

themes.title: Frontier Trees
themes.blurb: Centroid + data structure hybrids, auxiliary trees with DP, and path aggregates needing several techniques stacked together.
signals: All-paths aggregates with a heavy per-centroid computation.
Dynamic / offline tree queries combining decomposition and a structure.
Virtual tree + DP over a query-specific subtree.
themes.technique: Stack centroid decomposition / HLD / virtual trees with segment trees and DP; keep each layer's complexity in check.
themes.trap: Compounding log factors past the time limit; decomposition double-counting.
themes.goal: Compose multiple tree techniques correctly.

themes.title: Frontier Strings
themes.blurb: Suffix automaton/array combined with heavy data structures and DP. The hardest substring problems on Codeforces, where every component must be optimal.
signals: Substring statistics over the suffix-automaton with extra constraints.
Multi-pattern matching fused with counting.
Lexicographic + structural queries together.
themes.technique: Build the suffix automaton/array, then run DP / data structures over its DAG / LCP intervals; control constant factors.
themes.trap: Automaton edge cases; constant factor death.
themes.goal: Treat suffix structures as a base layer for harder logic.

themes.title: Frontier Counting
themes.blurb: Generating functions, advanced inclusion–exclusion, and counting over deeply structured objects. Long algebraic derivations that must be exactly right.
signals: Counts expressible as polynomial / power-series convolutions.
Several layers of inclusion–exclusion or symmetry.
Bijections that transform a hard count into an easy one.
themes.technique: Generating functions and convolutions; layered inclusion–exclusion; bijective reformulation; everything mod p with precomputed factorials.
themes.trap: A single sign or index error invalidating the whole derivation.
themes.goal: Carry a long counting derivation without error.

themes.title: Frontier Number Theory
themes.blurb: Deep multiplicative-function machinery, sublinear sieves, and group-structure tricks. Number theory at the level where the identity is a small theorem.
signals: Sublinear evaluation of a multiplicative sum.
Heavy Möbius / Dirichlet manipulation.
Order / discrete-log structure exploited deeply.
themes.technique: Sublinear sieves for prefix sums of multiplicative functions; Möbius/Dirichlet algebra; group structure for order-based counting.
themes.trap: Precision/overflow at scale; multiplicativity edge cases.
themes.goal: Apply sublinear number-theoretic machinery.

themes.title: Frontier Constructive
themes.blurb: The deepest constructive and interactive problems: a single elegant invariant or adaptive strategy, found only after long thought and proven airtight.
signals: 'Construct / interact …' with an extremely tight bound.
Adaptive judging that punishes any wasted query.
A beautiful answer that is invisible until the key idea lands.
themes.technique: Search for the one invariant or strategy that dominates; prove it fully; stress-test the construction exhaustively.
themes.trap: Plausible ideas that fail the bound — only a proof saves you here.
themes.goal: Find and prove the decisive constructive idea.
